messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 36
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Consultant
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 70

He is a 36-year-old North American man who comes across as careful, controlled, and quietly vigilant, the kind of person who seems to be listening for something even when the room is still. He has been married for several years and works as a tax consultant, a job that requires precision, long hours at a screen, and steady concentration through the pressures of deadlines and client demands. He describes himself as someone who used to take pride in being reliable, methodical, and hard to rattle. That sense of himself changed during his military service, where he was deployed in a setting that taught him to scan for danger before he ever allowed himself to feel it.

He does not speak at first about the worst moments directly. He circles them, as if approaching a live wire. Over time, the sequence becomes clearer: the days of heightened alertness, the blast that changes everything, the immediate shock of noise and dust and broken communication, the bodies on the ground, the urgent efforts to help, and the sense that the world has become permanently unstable in the span of a few seconds. He remembers the smell of smoke and metal, the gritty taste of debris, the sound of shouting that seemed to come from far away and too close at once. What stays with him most is not only what happened, but how fast it happened, how little time there was to think, and how quickly his body learned that danger could arrive without warning.

After the event, he returns home physically intact but internally altered. He expects that time and routine will restore him. Instead, ordinary life feels strangely thin and unreliable. He finds himself sitting with his back to walls in restaurants and watching entrances without meaning to. He notices cars too closely, startles when a truck backfires, and feels his shoulders tighten before he knows why. Sleep becomes broken and shallow. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes in the night already tense, as if his body has not been told that the danger is over. When he does drift off, his dreams pull him back into chaotic, fragmentary scenes of the deployment. He wakes sweaty, disoriented, and immediately alert, listening for sounds in the house. His wife learns not to touch him suddenly, because even a hand on his shoulder can make him flinch hard enough to embarrass him.

At work, he remains outwardly competent, but his concentration is not what it was. Tax season becomes especially punishing because the work demands sustained attention, patience with details, and calm under pressure. He can still handle numbers and deadlines, but he loses time in meetings because his mind drifts into scanning mode. A slammed file drawer or a raised voice in the office can send him into a wave of irritability that he later regrets. He rereads the same line repeatedly and sometimes cannot remember whether he has already answered a client’s question. He becomes more rigid with his schedule, more intolerant of interruptions, and more likely to work late because the structure helps him feel contained. Even then, he feels detached, as if he is performing his old life rather than fully living it.

His marriage carries much of the weight of his struggle. He loves his wife and wants to be present with her, but he often feels separated by an invisible pane of glass. When she asks how he is doing, he tends to say he is fine, because the alternative feels too exposed and too hard to explain. He notices her worry and feels ashamed of the distance his symptoms create. He pulls away from social plans, declines gatherings, and uses fatigue as a reason, though he also knows he is avoiding the unpredictability of being around people too long. In quieter moments, he admits that he feels guilty for surviving when others did not, and that the guilt returns most sharply when he is alone and the house is still.

He tries, in the way many disciplined people do, to push through. He exercises, organizes, overworks, and keeps his routines tight. For a while, this seems to help. But the effort costs him. When memories intrude, they come with the force of reliving rather than remembering. He can be in his office reviewing a client file and suddenly be back in the deployment, body braced, chest tight, pulse quickened, as if he has been yanked out of the present. He does not trust these shifts in his own mind. He feels frustrated that he is no longer the man who could absorb stress and move on. At the same time, there is a tired part of him that knows he has been carrying the event for years, long after everyone else has moved forward.

Recently, he has started to speak more plainly about how much effort it takes to get through a day. He still functions, still works, still shows up, but it is clear that much of his energy is spent managing the aftereffects of what happened over there. The military experience remains present in his body and mind, shaping his sleep, his alertness, his relationships, and even the way he moves through an ordinary office on an ordinary afternoon.
